title: Your Bedroom May Be Too Hot for Your Heart. A Study Found That Sleeping Above 26°C Nearly Triples the Risk of Reduced Cardiac Recovery.
excerpt: An Australian study of overnight bedroom temperatures found a dose-response relationship with heart rate variability. For South Asians — who already carry elevated cardiovascular risk — the implications are especially urgent as summer begins.
body:
As summer descends across the United States, millions of Indian Americans are cranking up the air conditioning and debating thermostat settings with their families. A growing body of research suggests those arguments may be more consequential than anyone thought — and that sleeping in a room that is even slightly too warm could be quietly stressing your heart.

The Study That Changed the Conversation

A study published in BMC Medicine by researchers at Griffith University in Queensland, Australia, tracked older adults across an entire summer, monitoring both their bedroom temperatures and their heart rate variability using wrist-worn fitness trackers and installed temperature sensors. The findings were striking.

Compared to nights when bedroom temperatures stayed below 24°C (75°F), sleeping in a room between 24°C and 26°C (75–79°F) increased the odds of reduced heart rate variability by 40 per cent. Between 26°C and 28°C (79–82°F), the odds doubled. And above 28°C (82°F), the odds nearly tripled.

Heart rate variability — the variation in time between heartbeats — is a marker of how well your autonomic nervous system is recovering overnight. Lower HRV is associated with increased sympathetic nervous system activity, essentially your body staying in fight-or-flight mode while you sleep instead of shifting into recovery.

"When the human body is exposed to heat, its normal physiological response is to increase the heart rate," said lead researcher Dr Fergus O'Connor. "The heart is working harder to try and circulate blood to the skin surface for cooling. When the heart works harder and for longer, it creates stress and limits our capacity to recover from the previous day's heat exposure."

Why This Matters More for South Asians

The implications for Indian Americans are compounded by what researchers already know about South Asian cardiovascular risk. A landmark study published in the Journal of the American Heart Association by Northwestern Medicine followed 2,700 adults and found that South Asians in the United States carry significantly higher rates of prediabetes, diabetes, and hypertension than white, Black, Hispanic, and Chinese adults — even when their diets, alcohol use, and exercise habits appeared healthier.

The mismatch was pronounced. By age 45, South Asian men and women had nearly double the prevalence of prediabetes compared to adults of other races. By age 55, they had the highest probability of developing diabetes of any group studied.

"The paradox tells us we're missing something fundamental to what is driving this elevated risk among South Asians," said Dr Namratha Kandula, professor of general internal medicine and epidemiology at Northwestern and the study's senior author.

If South Asians are already carrying a heavier cardiovascular burden, then any additional stressor — including chronically disrupted sleep from a warm bedroom — compounds an already elevated baseline risk.

The Practical Problem

Many Indian American households keep their thermostats higher at night to save on electricity, particularly in states like Texas, Arizona, and California where summer utility bills can be punishing. Others simply prefer warmer sleeping conditions, a habit carried from homes in India where air conditioning was a luxury or absent entirely.

But the research draws a clear line: the cardiovascular cost of sleeping in a warm room is measurable, cumulative, and potentially significant over time. There are no official guidelines for maximum nighttime bedroom temperatures in any country, a gap that Dr O'Connor's team specifically flagged.

What the Science Suggests You Do

Sleep researchers and cardiologists converge on a few evidence-based recommendations for the summer months:

Keep your bedroom between 18°C and 22°C (65–72°F). This is the range most consistently associated with optimal sleep quality and cardiac recovery. If air conditioning costs are a concern, a fan directed at the body can lower perceived temperature by several degrees.

Take a cool shower before bed, not a cold one. A study from the Centre for Interdisciplinary Research in Biology found that a moderately cool shower lowers core body temperature effectively, while an ice-cold shower can paradoxically trigger heat retention as the body overcompensates.

Monitor your resting heart rate and HRV if you wear a wearable. Oura rings, Apple Watches, and Fitbits all track HRV. A sustained drop in overnight HRV during summer months is a signal that your sleep environment may be too warm.

Hydrate before bed but not excessively. Sweating during sleep leads to dehydration, which further stresses the cardiovascular system. A small glass of water before bed helps, but too much disrupts sleep through bathroom trips.

The Bigger Picture

Climate change is making hot nights more frequent and more intense. In the United States, overnight low temperatures have been rising faster than daytime highs in many regions. For a community that already faces disproportionate cardiovascular risk, the bedroom thermostat is not a trivial household debate — it is a health decision with real, measurable consequences.

The next time someone in your family turns the AC down at night, they may be doing more for your heart than either of you realises.
